title: Cycling Nakhon Pathom: Phutthamonthon + Tha Chin River 2D1N
metaDesc: A laid-back 2-day cycling plan for Nakhon Pathom, Thailand: quiet loops at Phutthamonthon, riverside riding along the Tha Chin, Wat Rai Khing, Don Wai market, plus bike rentals, real food stops and the best times to go.
keywords: cycling Nakhon Pathom, Phutthamonthon cycling, Tha Chin River, Don Wai floating market, Wat Rai Khing
h1:
Cycling Phutthamonthon
+ the Tha Chin Riverside
intro: Nakhon Pathom is so close to Bangkok that a lot of people drive straight past it, but bring a bike and the place turns into a perfect weekend ride. Spend the morning rolling through the shady, quiet grounds of Phutthamonthon, then trace the Tha Chin River in the afternoon to pay respects at Wat Rai Khing and graze your way through riverside food at Don Wai market. This is a 2-day, 1-night plan that's easy on the legs, big on food, and full of river atmosphere.

blocks.html: The charm of cycling in Nakhon Pathom is that almost everything is flat — no steep climbs to wear out your legs. The main loop around the Phutthamonthon grounds runs roughly 8 kilometres, shaded by big old trees the whole way. Once you leave the grounds you can keep tracing the canals and the Tha Chin River, passing riverside temples, fruit orchards and old markets. It works for serious riders who want a proper workout and for families who just want to roll along and take it easy.

blocks.text: Before you set off — bikes and what to bring

blocks.html: The safest bet is to bring your own bike, because rental points in Nakhon Pathom still aren't as common as in the big tourist towns. If you drive in, you can park at the Phutthamonthon grounds and unload your bike right there. But if you don't have a bike of your own, there are still a few options.

items: Anywheel (bike-share app) — docking points are scattered around Mahidol University, Salaya, which sits right next to Phutthamonthon. Good for short rides around the area; charged by the minute in the app.
Sireepark, Mahidol Salaya — rents bikes and scooters for around THB 30/day, ideal for riding through the university's botanical garden.

HHBL (Happy and Healthy Bike Lane) — a rental and bike-storage shop with everything from hybrids at THB 420/4 hrs up to carbon road bikes at THB 920/4 hrs. Book ahead via Line @hhblbikerental to be safe.
What you should pack — helmet, drinking water, sunscreen and a buff, because the late-morning and afternoon sun in Nakhon Pathom is stronger than you'd expect.

blocks.title: The most comfortable time to ride
blocks.html: The Phutthamonthon grounds are shady, true, but between 6 and 9 in the morning it's cool and the quietest you'll find it — you can ride freely without dodging walkers. The evening, around 4 to 6 pm, is pretty too, but the crowds start building up.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Phutthamonthon in the morning, then along the river to Wat Rai Khing

blocks.html: Day one is all about getting your fill of riding the Phutthamonthon grounds in the morning, then easing down along the Tha Chin River toward Sam Phran, finishing at Wat Rai Khing and a riverside cafe in the afternoon.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Ride Phutthamonthon → Tha Chin riverside → Wat Rai Khing

items.activity: Start at the Phutthamonthon grounds, looping around the Phra Sri Sakayatossapholyan Buddha statue
items.note: The loop around the grounds is about 8 km, flat and shaded by big trees. Two laps is a nice warm-up, and the crowds are still thin.

items.activity: Break for a coffee, then walk over to photograph the Buddha statue and the Buddhist-history garden
items.note: There are rest spots and drink stalls dotted around the grounds. Top up your water before heading out on the longer route.

items.activity: Leave the grounds and ride along the canal and the riverside road following the Tha Chin down toward Sam Phran
items.note: Most of it is flat with some traffic. Keep left and watch the junction crossings. Around 12–15 km depending on the route you pick.

items.activity: Reach Wat Rai Khing, pay respects to Luang Pho Wat Rai Khing, and stop for lunch near the temple
items.note: The temple sits on the Tha Chin River — spacious and shady, with plenty of food and snack shops out front.

items.activity: Rest your legs at a riverside cafe
items.note: There are several cafes along the Tha Chin near Wat Rai Khing, like Neuk Cafe (open roughly 09:00–20:00), set among shady coconut groves. A good spot to rest before riding back.

items.activity: Ride back to your stay around Salaya / Phutthamonthon
items.note: Avoid riding after dark if your bike has no lights. Leaving the cafe before the late-afternoon light fades makes for an easier ride back.

blocks.title: A few honest words
blocks.html: Some stretches along the Tha Chin River are shared community roads with traffic, not separated bike lanes. If you're riding with small kids, it's better to stick mainly to the Phutthamonthon grounds and take the car to Wat Rai Khing and the floating market instead — it's safer that way.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Don Wai floating market, then an easy ride to close out the trip

blocks.html: Day two is lighter, built around eating and the atmosphere of an old riverside market. The Don Wai floating market sits inside Wat Don Wai, right on the Tha Chin River — an old-school market that's still buzzing, open daily from roughly 08:00–17:00, with so much food you'll need to pace your appetite.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Easy ride → Don Wai floating market → a long graze along the Tha Chin

items.activity: An easy lap or two around the Phutthamonthon grounds, catching the morning angles
items.note: No need to push it on the last day — ride to catch the morning light and loosen up before the eating starts.

items.activity: Ride or drive to Don Wai floating market, Wat Don Wai
items.note: If you ride, it's about 10–13 km from Phutthamonthon along community roads. Watch for traffic heading into the market and find parking or bike storage in front of the temple.

items.activity: Walk the market and try the famous riverside eats
items.note: Well-known spots include Nai Nap five-spice duck (closed Mondays), Suwannarat raft seafood on the river at THB 100–300 a plate, Nai Tue kuay jab, and Krua Baan Tia for boat noodles and pork leg.

items.activity: Sit down for lunch on a riverside raft over the Tha Chin
items.note: Suwannarat raft has a big menu of soups, stir-fries, curries, fried dishes and seafood, right over the water with a nice cool breeze.

items.activity: Finish with dessert — toddy-palm cake, Thai sweets, gifts to take home
items.note: Don Wai is known for toddy-palm cake, old-style Thai sweets, and bagged five-spice duck to take home — easy souvenirs to pick up.

items.activity: Ride or drive back, closing out the trip along the Tha Chin
items.note: If you've still got energy and time, swing by Sampran Riverside on the Tha Chin before heading back — a shady, green riverside garden.

blocks.text: Riverside Tha Chin stops you shouldn't skip

items.name: Wat Rai Khing
items.blurb: A temple on the Tha Chin River in Sam Phran district — spacious and shady, with a market and food shops out front. A popular stop to pay respects partway along the cycling route.

items.name: Don Wai Floating Market
items.blurb: An old market inside Wat Don Wai on the Tha Chin River, open daily around 08:00–17:00. Loads of food and several riverside rafts — the natural eating hub for day two.

items.name: Sampran Riverside
items.blurb: A conservation-focused attraction on the Tha Chin, with shady gardens — a nice place to pause or stroll before heading home.

items.name: Riverside cafes near Wat Rai Khing
items.blurb: Several cafes sit right on the river, like Neuk Cafe, set among coconut groves — good for resting your legs in the afternoon.

blocks.text: Loose ends — where to stay and getting there

blocks.html: Accommodation is easy to find around Salaya and Phutthamonthon, the closest options to the riding loop — wake up, walk out and you're on the bike. Coming from Bangkok, it's about a 30–45 minute drive from the Thonburi side to Phutthamonthon depending on traffic, and tossing your bike in the back of the car is the easiest way. Public transport has vans and buses to Salaya, but hauling a bike along is more of a hassle.

items: Stay around Salaya if you want to ride Phutthamonthon every morning — it's the shortest commute.
Check opening days before heading to Don Wai; some famous shops, like Nai Nap five-spice duck, close on Mondays.
Long weekends get busy — the floating market and Wat Rai Khing pack out on Saturdays and Sundays, so going early is easier.

faq.q: What do I need to prepare for cycling at Phutthamonthon?
faq.a: The safest bet is to bring your own bike, since rental points in Nakhon Pathom are still limited. If you don't have one, there's the Anywheel app around Mahidol Salaya, or you can rent from HHBL (hybrids from THB 420/4 hrs, book ahead via Line). Don't forget a helmet, drinking water and sunscreen.

faq.q: How long is the cycling loop at the Phutthamonthon grounds?
faq.a: The loop around the Buddha statue is about 8 kilometres, flat and shaded by big trees the whole way. Two laps comes to around 16 km, which is a good distance for most people.

faq.q: When is the most comfortable time to cycle in Nakhon Pathom?
faq.a: Mornings from 6 to 9 are best — cool, quiet and smooth riding. The evening, around 4 to 6 pm, looks pretty but the crowds start building. Avoid riding in the midday sun, which is strong.

faq.q: Which days is the Don Wai floating market open?
faq.a: It's open daily, roughly 08:00–17:00, inside Wat Don Wai on the Tha Chin River. But some famous shops, like Nai Nap five-spice duck, close on Mondays, so check ahead if you're coming specifically for one of them.

faq.q: Can I ride with small kids?
faq.a: Inside the Phutthamonthon grounds you can ride with kids easily, since it's flat and separated from the main roads. But some stretches along the Tha Chin River are shared community roads with traffic, so if you're bringing kids, stick to the grounds and take the car to Wat Rai Khing and the floating market instead.
